Main findings
In Semester 2, I extended the successful Iteration 1 priority-based selection approach with simulated annealing 
acceptance and a basin-hopping search, added prototype operational constraints, analysed search settings, and 
compared controlled starting schedules. The main recommendation is to retain priority-based selection with 
tuned neighbourhoods. The annealing experiments produced small smoothness gains but did not justify 
replacing the tuned baseline.
Worst-day availability 19 is impossible for the current forecast under the modelled maintenance rules. Six 
unavoidable D-check intervals overlap, limiting availability to 18. The priority method already reaches that 
bound. This establishes optimality for worst-day availability on this instance; it does not establish globally 
optimal smoothness.

1 Baseline and maintenance model
Iteration 1 established that prioritising checks on the worst availability days gives a practical deterministic 
search. The execution plan records an improvement from 15 to 18 aircraft and a runtime of approximately 15.4 
seconds. The later local tuning record reproduces the published baseline at 18 aircraft, standard deviation 
1.413971, and 14.6 seconds. I use those reproducible local scores for Semester 2 comparisons rather than 
combining rounded values from older slides. [S1, S2, S10]
Forecast and objective
Quantity Value
Aircraft 24
Maintenance checks 278 comprising A 144 B 72 C 38 D 24
Base date 21 January 2026
Forecast horizon Inclusive last day index 4480
Availability observations 4481 daily values for indices 0 through 4480
Total maintenance occupancy 10248 aircraft days
Average availability 21.713010 aircraft
The code scores schedules lexicographically: maximise worst-day availability first, minimise the standard 
deviation of daily availability second, and maximise mean availability third. Standard deviation uses the full daily 
series and the population convention in NumPy. A lower standard deviation means a smoother availability 
profile. A smoother schedule cannot outrank another schedule with better worst-day availability. [S2]
Maintenance rules
Check Duration days Interval days Early start allowance days
A 14 365 42
B 28 730 70
C 84 1460 70
D 126 2920 70
The sequence is A, B, A, C, A, B, A, D. A check can start within its legal start window and must not overlap 
another check on the same aircraft. When a check moves, the aircraft’s later checks are rebuilt using the interval 
reset rules. Larger checks reset the corresponding smaller-check clocks. The new start must lie inside the 
recalculated legal window, even when it moves later than its current start. A check cannot start after its due 
date, but it may finish after that date. [S2]
The baseline tries shifts of 28, 14, 7, and 3 days in either direction, in that order, with a 400-iteration cap. It 
searches the first priority level containing an improving neighbour and chooses the best improvement in that 
level. Availability is updated by removing the aircraft’s old maintenance intervals and adding the rebuilt ones. 
[S2]
Precision correction: older notes call the horizon 4480 days. The current code treats 4480 as an inclusive index and computes 4481 daily 
observations. The quoted means and standard deviations use those 4481 observations.

2 Integration of simulated annealing
The main integration is in savn_priority_sa.py. It reuses the baseline’s priority ordering, check rebuild, availability 
update, and scoring. The change is that feasible non-improving moves can enter the search. This matters 
because the original generate_neighbors function filters out every move that does not improve the score before 
an acceptance rule can see it. [S2, S3]
Function Role
generate_feasible_neighbors Proposes legal moves from the first priority level with feasible neighbours including 
non-improvements
accept_candidate Applies temperature acceptance or the tightened rule
savn_optimise Runs classic single-chain simulated annealing with cooling
greedy_polish Runs deterministic improvement search with optional tabu and operational filters
basin_hopping_optimise Combines warm start escape walk and tabu polish
start_vector and is_tabu_neighbor Identify and reject the exact pre-escape schedule during polish
Classic simulated annealing
The classic SA function warm-starts from the published priority baseline by default, proposes a random feasible 
neighbour, applies the acceptance test, and multiplies temperature by cooling_rate after each iteration. The 
default temperature is 1.0 and the default cooling rate is 0.95. It stores a current schedule for exploration and a 
separate best-so-far schedule for reporting. This version contains the cooling mechanism described in the plan. 
[S3]
Acceptance rule
An improvement in the ranked score is accepted immediately. For a non-improving score, the loss is measured 
on the first worsened component: aircraft lost on the worst day, otherwise the increase in standard deviation, 
otherwise the decrease in average availability. The acceptance probability is the exponential of negative loss 
divided by temperature. At nonpositive temperature the code rejects non-improvements. At positive 
temperature an exact score tie has zero loss and is accepted. [S3]
The tightened option rejects a lower worst-day availability before the temperature test. The usual candidate 
permits a temporary reduction in worst-day availability, while retaining the best-so-far result. Every proposed 
move still has to satisfy maintenance rules and any active operational constraints. Temperature changes 
acceptance of legal schedules; it does not legalise a prohibited check movement. [S3, S4]
Difference from the execution plan
Slide 6 says that a lower worst day is always rejected. The later recorded decision allows that loss in the 
candidate and keeps the stricter rule as a fallback. Slide 4 describes cooling, which applies to classic SA. The 
measured basin-hopping candidate instead uses a fixed escape temperature throughout each run. Those 
distinctions should be stated in the upcoming presentation. [S1, S3, S8]

3 Basin hopping and earlier experiments
After classic SA failed to improve the published baseline, the search developed into basin-hopping with tabu 
polish. It first runs priority-based polish. Each escape cycle restarts from the protected best-so-far schedule, 
deliberately seeks a legal move with lower worst-day availability, then makes a plateau walk before polishing 
again. The exact pre-escape start vector is temporarily tabu during that polish so the search cannot immediately 
restore the same schedule. Only an improved polished result replaces best-so-far. [S3, S9]
The final decision settings use escape temperature 1.5, 15 escape cycles, 30 plateau moves, and up to 400 polish 
iterations. The escape loop permits one initial move plus up to 30 subsequent moves per cycle. There is no 
cooling of escape_temperature in basin_hopping_optimise. The settling stage is deterministic polish. [S3]

Interpretation
The gain is real in the saved best-so-far scores, but it is small compared with the extra search effort. The

The timeout checks occur between iterations and escape moves rather than inside neighbour evaluation. A long 
evaluation can therefore overrun the nominal 300-second limit. The recorded overshoots range up to 721.3 
seconds in the settings sweep. The measured elapsed time and timeout flag, rather than a claim of an exact five￾minute cap, should be reported. [S3, S6, S7]
All tightened runs match the tuned baseline. In the present basin-hopping implementation the first escape move 
must lower worst-day availability, while tightened acceptance forbids that move. Thus the tightened option 
cannot start its escape phase and effectively returns the warm-start polish. Its shorter recorded times do not 
show a new successful annealing search. [S3]

5 Why worst day availability 19 is impossible
This result follows from mandatory maintenance occupancy. It is independent of how many random seeds or 
parameter combinations are tried. The current workbook contains 24 aircraft. Guaranteeing availability 19 would 
require no more than five aircraft in maintenance on every day. [S2, S5, S15]
Unavoidable interval of a D check
A first D check lasts 126 days and may start from 70 days before its due date through to its due date. The earliest 
placement finishes 56 days after due; the latest placement begins on due. Every legal placement therefore 
covers the 56-day interval from the due date to 56 days after it, with the end date excluded. In the report 
notation this is [due, due + 56).
The first D due date is fixed by the opening due date plus 7 times 365 days. Earlier A, B, or C checks do not reset 
the D clock. Moving earlier checks cannot remove the first D’s unavoidable interval. The loaded first-D windows 
agree with those reconstructed from the opening due dates for all 24 aircraft. [S2, S5]
Aircraft Unavoidable overlap
Aircraft 11 20 to 25 May 2033
Aircraft 14 20 to 25 May 2033
Aircraft 15 20 to 25 May 2033
Aircraft 19 20 to 25 May 2033
Aircraft 24 20 to 25 May 2033
Blue-8 20 to 25 May 2033
The six intervals coincide on day indices 2676 through 2681, corresponding to 20 through 25 May 2033. At least 
six aircraft must be down on those days, so availability can be no greater than 24 minus 6, which is 18. 
Consequently a worst-day availability of 19 is infeasible for this forecast and these rules. The baseline’s achieved 
value of 18 matches the upper bound. [S5, S15]
What the bound does and does not establish
Total downtime is 10248 aircraft days. Across 4481 daily observations, average maintenance load is 2.286990 
aircraft. That is below the five-aircraft-down allowance implied by target 19. The failure comes from 
concentrated unavoidable occupancy rather than insufficient average capacity.
The bound is conditional on the fleet, check durations, early-start allowances, and fixed opening due dates. 
Reaching 19 would require changing the instance or one of those assumptions. It cannot be achieved by tuning 
this optimiser alone. The model does not impose hangar-bay, crew, or parts capacity limits, so those are not the 
cause of this bound. [S2, S15]
The D-core overlap, dates, aircraft names, workbook counts, and loaded schedule compliance were independently recalculated from the
current local workbook during preparation of this report.

6 Operational constraints and measured outcomes
The operational prototype adds three hard rules in a separate JSON configuration. A busy period requires a 
minimum number of aircraft available within an inclusive date range. A displacement limit bounds the absolute 
movement of each check from its as-loaded start, including changes caused by rebuilding later checks. A 
dependency group requires a stated number of its named aircraft to remain available on every day. [S4, S16]
The rules are dummy scenarios for research. The canonical maintenance workbook remains the input. Both 
feasible-neighbour generation and greedy polish can apply the operational filter. A hotter temperature never 
overrides an operational breach. The loaded schedule is checked first and a scenario that it already breaks is 
rejected without a repair search. [S3, S4, S6]

comparison runs are not present in the latest result file, even though the filtering interface supports them. [S1,

7 Priority method hyperparameter analysis
The local priority-method study contains 74 trials and records total elapsed time 3151.2 seconds, about 52.5

Keep the first-priority-level selection policy and the 400-iteration cap. The winner accepts 319 moves and 
reduces standard deviation by 0.022111, approximately 1.56%, against the published baseline. The default stops 
after 280 accepted moves. Increasing its cap to 800 reproduces the same result, while cutting it to 160 leaves

Large shifts first and layered neighbourhoods matter on this instance. Single small offsets and small-first ordering 
can consume the iteration budget before reaching 18. Collapsing every offset into one union is worse than the 
half-step ladder. Searching every priority level does not beat the current selection policy. These are measured 
instance-specific findings, not universal rules for all fleets. [S10]
Use the tuned neighbourhoods through greedy_polish or a caller that accepts shift_sets. The published baseline savn_optimise function 
itself does not expose a shift_sets argument and its original defaults remain the reproducibility reference. [S2, S3, S4]

9 Compact staggered and as loaded starts
This experiment addresses whether an initially staggered schedule differs from a compact overlapping schedule 
and the current as-loaded schedule. The implemented labels are bunched for compact, spread for staggered, and 
as-loaded for the current forecast. Each method runs from the same constructed start, without operational 
limits, so the measured start effect is not mixed with constraint effects. [S4, S6, S7]
Construction of the three starts
The opening check is pinned to its due date by the maintenance replay. The implemented variants therefore 
move check index 1, the next check on each aircraft. Bunched moves it toward the fleet median start, clamped 
inside its legal window. Spread selects the legal-window endpoint furthest from that median. Each aircraft’s later 
checks are then rebuilt. The compact case aims to cluster checks across aircraft; it never permits overlapping 
checks on the same aircraft. [S2, S4]

a controlled test of the implemented start constructor, rather than a redesign of opening maintenance ages or a 
globally maximally compact or maximally staggered fleet. [S2, S4, S5]

Validation already represented in the project
The source includes tests for baseline maintenance replay, acceptance decisions, feasible neighbours, seeded 
behaviour, best-so-far protection, tabu polish, operational limits, start construction, and the numeric keep-or￾drop rule. The priority tuning records explicitly mark all 74 schedules as rule compliant. The final study results

maintenance rules and dummy limits, rather than all requirements of a deployed fleet planning system. [S10,

Remaining work before broader claims
For a complete comparison under operational limits, measure candidate runs on the loose and medium 
scenarios using the same neighbourhoods, start, runtime rule, and fixed seeds as priority polish. Keep the tight 
result labelled as an invalid loaded start unless a repair search or a separate feasibility analysis is performed.
For stronger evidence on initial stagger, define a quantitative measure of compactness or overlap before 
constructing more extreme starts. Repeat candidate runs across seeds if the aim is a robust stochastic 
comparison. If starting maintenance ages or opening due dates are changed, treat those as a different instance 
and recompute the forced-core bound.
For performance claims, reduce deadline overshoot and measure runs in a consistent environment. The 
deterministic tuned baseline has the same score but different recorded timings of 96.5, 115.6, and 63.3 seconds 
across study contexts. Thus the available timing ratio describes the decision records, not an isolated hardware￾controlled speed benchmark.
Presentation corrections
Explain that the tested candidate can temporarily lower worst-day availability, uses fixed escape temperature, 
and returns best-so-far. Distinguish the proof that 19 is impossible from the rejection of the tight loaded start. 
Use the local JSON values instead of mixing old slide metrics or the regenerated cloud dataset. The source 
handover filename includes 30 October, but it is an existing report label; the current evidence snapshot is the 
local results available on 12 October 2026. [S1, S3, S7, S21]

11 Suggested presentation narrative
Iteration 1 foundation
“At the end of Iteration 1, priority-based selection gave us a practical method. It targeted the checks that 
affected our worst availability days, rebuilt each aircraft’s later checks when a move occurred, and updated the 
availability efficiently. On the local forecast it improved worst-day availability from 15 to 18 aircraft.”
What I added in Semester 2
“In Semester 2, I investigated whether allowing temporary worse moves could improve the result further. I 
retained the maintenance logic and the priority search. First I added classic simulated annealing acceptance. I 
then developed basin-hopping, where the search leaves a good schedule, walks through a different region, and 
uses priority polish to improve it again. The best schedule is protected throughout.”
What the experiments showed
“Classic simulated annealing did not improve the published baseline in the three recorded local runs. Basin￾hopping did improve smoothness slightly, but the improvement became much smaller once I compared it fairly 
with a tuned priority method. The tuned priority result was 1.391860 standard deviation. The median basin￾hopping result was 1.390417, about a 0.10 percent reduction. Two of the three runs timed out, and the median 
runtime exceeded five minutes. That does not meet the adoption rule.”
Why I stopped chasing availability 19
“I also established a bound on this forecast. A D check lasts 126 days but can only start up to 70 days early. That 
leaves 56 days when it must be in maintenance regardless of its legal start. Six aircraft share that unavoidable 
interval on 20 to 25 May 2033. With 24 aircraft, availability can only be 18 on those days. The baseline therefore 
reaches the best possible worst-day availability under these rules.”
Constraints and settings
“I added dummy busy periods, displacement limits, and dependency groups as hard rules. Loose and medium 
scenarios kept legal priority schedules at 18, although smoothing became harder. The tight pack was already 
invalid on the loaded plan, and this prototype does not repair it. In the 74-trial priority settings study, richer half￾step neighbourhoods gave the strongest dependable gain, approximately 1.56 percent better smoothness than 
the original settings.”
Starting schedule and recommendation
“I compared compact, staggered, and as-loaded starts. The first check cannot move in this model, so these 
variants alter the next check and rebuild the later checks. All methods reached 18, but as-loaded gave the 
smoothest final result. This shows that the starting schedule matters, and simply spreading the next checks does 
not guarantee a better final plan. My recommendation is to retain priority-based selection with the tuned half￾step neighbourhoods. The Semester 2 contribution is the measured comparison, the availability bound, the 
operational prototype, and the sensitivity evidence supporting that choice.”
This narrative describes the recorded experiments. Do not describe the candidate as cooling over time or the tight scenario as globally 
impossible without additional analysis.
